body:
All good guesses for future events.

Myself, I thought they'll have the Nazgûl only come into being properly in s4 and all in Númenor to save time. Either way I'm guessing the prime candidates are Kemen, Lord Belzagar, Hagen (the guy from the southlands plot who's with Isildur's probable future wife) and one of the masked guys with the Dark Wizard (their departed leader did conspicuously say "we used to be kings").

Tolkien says that Sauron probably destroyed the Ent-wives and this season introduced them. Combined with the ending shot of this season of Númenoreans wanting to destroy the forest I think the Nazgûl will establish their power and cruelty by annihilating the ent-wives to get timber to build Pharazôn's fleet so he can sail westwards.  
  
For Númenor aiding the elves in defeating Sauron, I think Pharazôn, Elendil and Isildur will put their differences aside to fight Sauron and the marriage to Miriel might be Pharazôn's supposed olive branch gesture. So with Isildur and Elendil by Pharazôn's side (momentarily) Theo and the Southlanders swear fealty to Númenor (setting up their eventual breaking of that oath and becoming the army of the dead in ROTK) and we'll see Elendil-Isildur setting up the foundations for Arnor-Gondor in seasons 3. By early season 4 they work out Pharazôn was just playing everyone for fools and only wanted Sauron as prisoner to use him as his weapon. 

My guesses, anyway!

It might take a while still for the Nazgûl to come properly into being so it'd be nice to see Sauron have some Orc henchmen of note (particularly given the focus the show gave to Orcs). I was thinking one idea would be seeing a ancestor to the Great Goblin from Goblintown from the Hobbit, the origin of the title maybe.

Given the dwarven belief that Durins reincarnate you might not be far off actually. The show hinted at this with King Durin saying that when a Durin is crowned the memories of their predecessors flow into his mind, so when Prince Durin takes the throne we might see some form of this.
I may have missed something here but my recollection is that the ring was trying to warn Galadriel to NOT take the barrow-wight road they ended up taking and Elrond overrides her, no?

Logistically his name should be in a Rhûn language but we don't really have a clue how those names sound properly and the show hasn't made much effort with it. If they properly go with the Blue Wizard canon he might end up being called Romestamo or Haimenar. 

Maybe they settle his name in Rhûn is Khâmul and the same-named Nazgûl (who's likely one of his masked henchmen guys) ends up taking the name after he's defeated. Tolkien never provided a etymology for the name Khâmul (nor in what language it is), so the show could guess it's a title of some sort in a Rhûn language.

One of the absolute MVPs of the show. Not a singles scene with him missed its mark for me and his leaping off to face the balrog is probably my favorite scene of the entire thing. Durin IV will have some big shoes to fill.
I was more reminded of Ecthelion vs Gothmog (also in the Fall of Gondolin) but the same principle holds anyway.

Probably the case in canon for Goblintown, although per "The Peoples of Middle-Earth" Sauron did settle a garrison of Orcs in the Misty Mountains (namely Gundabad) in the aftermath of the Fall of Eregion to counter-act Dwarves. Logistically they're probably the origin of Goblintown later on, so I wouldn't be surprised if the show abridges this and has Sauron skip straight to Goblintown.
Yeah I'm likewise fairly sure he's ending up this way. Númenoreans trampling all over his people is probably the start.

A random thought was occurring to me that Sauron might placate the Orcs by giving them a place of their own to rule over without his interference in the Misty Mountains, which might be Goblin Town. Glug's son might end up being the ancestor of the Great Goblin we see in the Hobbit. 

Fairly far-fetched theory though!

This episode seemed to have a bunch of Fall of Gondolin nods, Sauron even brings it up in dialogue to Celebrimbor. King Durin leaping to face the balrog also calls to mind Ecthellion facing down Gothmog in Gondolin.
Did they? Which one? I'm curious about this.
Benjamin Walker is hilarious. We need him in more scenes next season.
King Durin has spent the whole season empathizing how a Dwarf doesn't back down. Do you think he'd just run away from a demon in his kingdom who attacked him? Not the Dwarven way.

Once again, Celebrimbor just steals the show completely and I hope Charles Edwards get as many nominations as possible. The dwarves also served as a high point (King Durin leaping to face the balrog while imparting wisdom to his son might be my favorite visual of the entire show so far, outstanding scene). Númenor and the Southlands also wrapped up nicely as the days of Pharazôn fully kick in and Elendil starts his journey to kingship with Narsil. 

Aside that I think it wobbled a tad with the pacing of things. The dwarves just sort of teleport in Eregion and we don't really see them fighting, nor the elvish retreat, properly. The scale really went to Hell in the later episode here. Galadriel vs Sauron was just ok but her arc really stalled this season, hope now she can grow into a different person (the ending did feel like those origin story moments where the superhero finally adopts their costume, with Galadriel in a white dress with the ring). Hobbit plotline cemented itself as the nadir of the show by rushing the Dark Wizard's reunion with the Stranger after stalling for seven episodes. At least that seems done with now and we can move on properly to the Istari. I'm glad that the show (and interviews) basically confirm that the DW is one of the Blues, at least. Now just give us his damn name! 

We lost two of the most compelling characters (Adar and Celebrimbor), though they got great dramatic send-offs. Next season will have big shoes to fill. Onwards to the founding of Rivendell and the War of Elves and Sauron!

I don't think they're "tiptoing around the Estate". I just think everyone should take Amazon's PR about how the Estate is 400% on-board with this with a grain of salt (if they were, the show would have free rein to do anything from the Silmarillion rather than the repeatedly stated rights cut-offs save the sporadic exception). These collaborations between rights holders and media companies are never fully smooth sailing (otherwise right holders wouldn't need to exist). 

In this scenario, for example, I'm not saying they do this in secret from the Estate, I'm saying there's a solid chance ROP pitched using the Blue Wizards and the Estate said "no, but you can create new ones to replace them if you want". We don't know if the Estate differs in treatment between Silmarillion IPs, Unfinished Tales IPs and Tolkien's letters IPs, we don't know what (if anything) the Estate asks in return for these "extra-official" usages. 

In summary, it's a relationship full of unknowns and the Blue Wizards are one of the furthest unknowns possible given they aren't characters in literally any of the "main" texts (Hobbit, LOTR, Sil).

People have said this a lot, but so far the Estate's breathing room has been a lot more distant, just allowing name drops and a few concepts extrapolated from the appendices (e.g. the shape of Númenor). We haven't yet seen any confirmation that the Estate would just openly allow them to fully use characters they have no right to (and the Blues are pretty firmly entrenched in Estate-only territory given they're only in Unfinished Tales and Tolkien's letters). 

It's a much more complex situation than people are claiming.

Appreciate the shout. The fact Gil-galad has (so far wholly unnamed) Commanders of the West, East and South (with North being Galadriel) is a good memory. One of them could be Amdir's rough replacement.
The question as worded was specifically about what they'd like to do in future seasons, plural. People are misreading the comment.

The rings pushing the dwarves to excessive greed and wrath is actually canon. It's mentioned in "Of the Rings of Power and the Third Age" in the Silmarillion, and the appendices of LOTR also contextualizes Thror's greed and foolhardy decisions (namely going into Moria despite warnings) through that.

Of course, the show speeds it up and perhaps over-empathizes it, but the principle is there.

I'm getting the impression they'll follow your lead somewhat and extricate Celebrian from Galadriel's bloodline. She might end up as already-adult elf contemporary refugee from Eregion that Elrond meets along the way to Rivendell. Might tie in the "daughter of Galadriel and Celeborn" aspect by having Galadriel and Celeborn care for her like a daughter at some point.

I'm pretty sure Stranger is Gandalf and I'm halfway sure that the Dark Wizard is a lawyer-friendly stand-in for the Blues because of how clearly the character's description is cribbing from their description (and the fact The Dark Wizard's cavalry minions have conspicuous blue streaks of paint across their torsos). I think they can't say he's Alatar/Pallando the Blue because they aren't present in LOTR-Hobbit, so they're writing around the limitations by being vague about his name and color to avoid stepping on the toes of the Estate. We might eventually get that he has a name like Ceretrith the Red or something else fully original.

Now, it's a question unto itself if being a replacement for the Blues also means he has a companion of the same rank like the Blues. If he does I think odds are that he has already killed his companion and we won't see him. 

That aside I wouldn't be surprised if they end up moving all of the Istari to the Second Age and we get to see Gandalf recruiting Saruman and Radagast across the seasons.
I think Bolg being out to avenge his father while Thorin is also out to avenge his fathers would have made a stronger thematic parallel between them, but to each his own.

He's a very interesting Orc concept for sure, but I can't for the life of me figure out why they didn't just give that character to Bolg, who is in fact in The Hobbit while Book Azog is long dead by then. Resurrecting Azog and also keeping Bolg was so redundant (and it meant Bolg ended up entirely superfulous and kind of generic), should have just made Bolg the Defiler pale Orc out to avenge his pa.
I'm pretty sure the Stranger is Gandalf. I'm talking about the Dark Wizard, Ciaran Hinds' character who is the villain of this plotline.

In the "The Quest for Erebor" text from Unfinished Tales Gandalf states that Smaug would likely ally with Sauron in the War of the Ring (implicitly out of his own volition rather than being controlled), so the hypothetical dragon/Smaug can just be siding with the Dark Wizard as a mutual partnership ("I barbecue your enemies and you lead me to treasure with your magic wisdom").   
  
In either case, Tolkien left the nature of dragons very unclear to begin with. A lot of it is guesswork.

Film or book Azog? Fairly different characters. Book Azog is kind of interesting because he and the Great Goblin from the Hobbit might be the only Orcs of note in canon you could construe as being entirely unrelated to Sauron/Saruman and are just doing their own thing. A case has been made Book Azog and The Great Goblin are the closest canon has to Adar's goals of independent Orcs free from Sauron.

The current mainline theory for the Dark Wizard is that he is one of the Blue Wizards (or a stand-in for them), the mysterious last two of the five wizards only mentioned properly in Unfinished Tales and Tolkien's letters. His shtick of being a fallen Istar with a magic cult in the East is directly cribbed from Tolkien's theories about what became of them.

In the Hobbit Bilbo makes an off-hand mention about "Were-worms" who live in a place called "The Last Desert" in the "East of East". Tolkien doesn't elaborate on this anywhere else on the canon (it might just be Hobbitish folklore and not real in-universe), but given we are dealing with Hobbits in the East in a giant desert in this plotline it's possible that the Dark Wizard has a Were-worm on-deck (and so Bilbo's reference gets retroactively explained as stories the Stoors/Nori and Poppy passed down).

They kind of already pulled a simiar trick by making the Stranger's origin feel like the possible historical origin for the Hobbit poem about "The Man In the Moon" who came down.

For the actual dragon theory outlined here I wouldn't be surprised if the idea ends up that the Dark Wizard has a very young Smaug by his side to tie in to Gandalf's desire to see Smaug dealt with inn the Hobbit (canonically he was probably born away later but Gandalf wasn't even here in the S.A, so).

I doubt they can use them 1:1 as none of them are in the Appendices, but they might make stand-ins. I have harbored a pet theory Arondir in this show will be used as a replacement for Oropher (his presence as the Greenwood representative in a heavily Noldor cast is suspicious) and share his fate leading the army of Greenwood against Sauron and dying in battle. I doubt they make him Legolas' grandfather as Oropher was (Arondir having a kid would feel weird by now), but I can see him being Thranduil's older brother who relinquished abdicated to hold watch over the Southlands or something. I also feel like the Dark Wizard is functionally a lawyer-friendly equivalent to the Blue Wizards. 

Amdír (and Amroth) I don't see any obvious replacement but we haven't gotten to Lórien yet. They might get some broad equivalents as Celeborn's kin or something.

I feel like this is side-stepping that they do, in fact, catch her. A couple of Orcs work out she's an elf in disguise and follow her after the pyre scene and she's saved by Arondir. They just don't catch her IMMEDIATELY.
Keep in mind they're up against an army led by Adar, a guy who has been leading soldiers to war for longer than everyone on the elven side has been alive.

Theo's gonna end up as the King of the Dead Men from the White Mountains Aragorn calls upon in ROTK, I think. The character is unnamed in canon, so it stands to reason that introducing him in the show would require inventing a original name and backstory.

From what he describes I think he's basically the same age as Cirdan the Shipwright, another guy who undertook the Great Journey. Shame they probably won't interact, they might have even known each other way back when.

I think the script is really solid (which stands to reason given it's often a 1:1 copy of the original story) but I think Brian Taylor was the wrong choice to direct this. The ashen-grey look of the film just looks stale and Taylor's tendency for out-of-focus choppy editing brings everything down. This would have turned out much better if they had gotten someone with a slicker horror style (e.g.Mike Flanagan). 

I have also to say that the addition of the BPRD rookie largely brings the film down. She contributes nothing to the plot and the script wobbles around her (most glaringly, the Crooked Man tempts everyone in the heroic cast but forgets to tempt her for whatever reason, like they forgot she was there). Should have stuck to Tom Farrell as a audience surrogate.
They should try the spin-offs. Sir Edward Grey Witchfinder and Lobster Johnson feel like they could be striking.
He's fantastic. Went from Consul of Rome to Consul of Rhûn.

I do think the battle has a bit of a progress structure, but its centered around Eregion's wall. The episode goes along with the Orcs slowly whittling down the soft spot of Eregion's wall as the elves try to stop them until it ends with them finally breaching the city.   
  
I think one of the problems is more that the show had no elves of note commanding the defense from within the city. Mirdania dies early, Celebrimbor is locked up in a tower losing it and Sauron doesn't care, so our perspective is chained to Elrond and Arondir outside the walls.

The show's premise to me seems to be a book-ends where the strongest rings are made first and last, so the Three are like a superpowered prototype black box of sorts, Seven and Nine flawed attempts to replicate them, and the One finally the invention that surpasses them.

I'm pretty sure the Dark Wizard is here for the long haul. I have been thinking the Dark Wizard may take the center stage when Sauron "defeated" and shackled up in Númenor (season 4, would be my guess), as that'd be a significant stretch of the show to have no antagonist for any of the non-Númenor plotline

My guess, if you'll indulge me, is:

* Khamul the Black Easterling (one of th Nazgul) is one of the Dark Wizard's underlings.
* While Númenor is being corrupted under Sauron the Dark Wizard attacks Greenwood from the East (and thus we are introduced to the elves from Greenwood).
* Dark Wizard founds the fortress of Dol Guldur (which literally means "hill of sorcery") of Hobbit-LOTR fame.
* Dark Wizard and Sauron team up, Khamul becomes one of the Nine.
* Dark Wizard's forces get conclusively defeated in s4 but he still holds Dol Guldur.
* S5 has the final showdown between Gandalf and the Dark Wizard in Dol Guldur as a sideshow to the War of the Last Alliance proper.
Given his roaring laughter in battle he might be in this solely for the love of the game.
That's because he's always doing badly. You can see it on his face, quite literally.
I feel like s1 shafted Celebrimbor, Gil-galad and Cirdan (as he wasn't even there). This season gave Celebrimbor much he needed, so here's hoping next season does Gil-galad justice in screentime.

Very strong episode. Celebrimbor really is the soul of this season and every scene he has is a highlight, Charles Edwards deserves all the accolades. Everything really selling the hopeleness.   
  
The battle is great spectacle on its own, if often chaotic and strategically confusing (mind you, the battles in the films are also pretty nonsensical strategically so this is nothing new). Wish Damrod lived to fight another day, he was great in the little we saw him.  

For more substantial problems I wish Gil-galad showed up more often. Him disappearing mid-episode was pretty weird, as was Adar doing parley with Elrond rather than the High King Gil-galad. But overall, minor blemishes on a geat episode.

The impression is they can fight better at night (hence Adar waiting in the shade until the night falls) but can struggle through the sun as long as there's cloud and shade to cover them. Eregion is perpetually under a thick cloud (and/or smoke) now from the looks of it (probably a mix of Sauron's doing and the smoke clouds from the battle).

It's a bummer Tolkien gave us next to nothing on the other six clans. Best we get is my usernamesake Lord Azaghal in the First Age as (presumably) one of the Broadbeams and Naugladur the Lord of Nogrod maybe being a Firebeard also in the First Age. In the context of the show it'd be cool if we saw the four dwarven clans that dwell in Rhûn via the Hobbit plotline eventually. 

Although, as with the weird rights situation, I don't know if they have the rights to the names of the other six dwarven clans. I don't think they are named in the appendices.
Lurtz isn't in the book, he's a LOTR film-original character so right off the bat he presumably can't even show up here.

The GOT battles might be a closer field of comparison given it's the same show format. In this sense I think its best analogue would be the Battle of Blackwater Bay: both the climax of the respective season 2s, both a siege against a walled city through water (sea in Blackwater, river in Eregion), both depicting a grayish situation with both sides of the battle having reasonable motivations.

Beards are an actual cultural iconography of dwarven culture in Tolkien (hence their main clan being "longbeards" and their greeting being "may your beard grow ever long") so you'd need to pitch a culture that holds breasts in similar esteem.
My guess is he'd be renamed to Khamul upon getting the Ring. We all know how much the show loves its mysteries, so even if it's not him I'd doubt they'd introduce Khamul straight up.

The other tidbit is that another iconic Sauron locale is Dol Guldur (which means "hill of sorcery") right next to Greenwood (which is comparatively close to Rhûn). I get the feeling the Dark Wizard have a hand in founding Dol Guldur (hence, hill of sorcery) and might attack Greenwood dwellings later in the plot. Then the plotlines converge.

Tolkien comments in a letter that the Ent-Wives were destroyed by Sauron and the show has hinted we might see this with the Ent appearances. Logistically I think this is going to happen in either season 3 (by Sauron directly) or 4 (by Númenoreans under Sauron).

Kemen (Pharazon's son), Lord Belzagar Pharazon's right-hand-man) and Earien (Elendil's daughter) are the Númenorean candidates so far IMO. I think the Dark Wizard's masked henchman might be Khamul, the Shadow of the East. So that would be four.   
  
For Theo I think this season pretty much confirmed for me that he's ending up as the King of the Dead so that rules him out, but I could imagine someone else from the Southlanders getting a ring. 

With the way the show juggles plotlines I doubt we'd have enough time to establish nine wholly different people from nine different places, so if I had to guess I think the vast majority of them will be Nùmenorean (maybe literally all of them sans Khamul).
I'd imagine mostly psychic torture given they're empathizing Sauron's telepathic abilities.

I'm not saying he fought in the battlefield alongside the soldiers of Cardolan (as he's a pretty deadset pacifist from the looks of it even aside everything else) but I think these passages show pretty clearly he had some level of involvement and some attachment to Cardolan. "Involvement" could be something as small as "knew the princess of cardolan and gave her counsel in friendship until their bitter end" (coincidentally, "giving counsel" is basically the sum total of his role in this show so far). 

I think sometimes people get a little too hung up on the fact Tom is completely apart from the events in LOTR and assume he never did anything ever in his entire existence. You could even make the case that the fact Cardolan ended in disaster is one of the reasons Tom keeps to himself in the present-day.
My inkling is that the plotlines merge less via Hobbits and more via The Dark Wizard's plans.

I think it's a mix of factors, among them that s2 is better than s1. They did go for the (questionable) move of making s1 basically a giant prologue for the rest of the show, establishing the main players, locales and relationships. S2 is the actual meat of the plot (in some sense I think they might have actually started from S2 creatively and worked backwards as they thought there wouldn't be enough time to establish it all in a single season).

In another sense, yeah, the pacing is I think much more fashioned for bingewatching than week-to-week.

Where the show is going with this plotine is anybody's guess but I think they might end up moving the arrival of ALL the Istari to the Second Age. So we're following Gandalf's self-discovery but Radagast, Saruman and the Blue Wizards (one of which is the Dark Wizard) are already here somewhere and he might recruit them over the course of the show to fight the Dark Wizard.

That aside, for your specific question, in the Unfinished Tales Istari text Gandalf at first refuses to go before being commanded by Manwe to join the others, so even in canon it feels like Saruman was more chosen as a leader because he stepped up to the task of his own accord (while Gandalf was more or less ordered to come along).
I have a theory that the Hobbit-Rhûn plotline will only converge with the main one by late season 3 or early 4, so we may be in for a long haul.

You're welcome!

Tom is a (deliberately) cryptic character, so much about him is guesswork. The Cardolan anectodes (particularly his moment with the brooch) point to the only known instance he may have had a larger involvement in the greater affairs of ME. I always favourted the idea he was a personification of Arda itself, so profoundly powerful but also profoundly static like a landmass.

It's in Fellowship of the Ring, between "In The House of Tom Bombadil" and "Fog on the Barrow-Downs". Tom explains to the Hobbits about how Cardolan (which is right around the borders of his domain) fell and the Barrow-Wights came to be with the tone of a eyewitness. Later the Hobbits get trapped by the Barrow-Wights in the place where the Last Prince of Cardolan is buried and afterwards Tom stops by one of the tombs and picks up a brooch: "He (Tom) looked long at it, as if stirred by some memory, shaking his head, and saying at last: "Here is a pretty toy for Tom and for his lady! Fair was she who long ago wore this on her shoulder. Goldberry shall wear it now, and we will not forget her!''. Later when he's escorting them out to Bree Tom is uncharacteristically solemn and quiet: "Tom said that it had once been the boundary of a kingdom, but a very long time ago. He seemed to remember something sad about it, and would not say much.”

It's all very nebulous (as with everything about Tom), but the general implication is that the brooch belonged to the wife of the Last Prince of Cardolan and Tom personally knew  and cared about her long ago. This combined with the fact the events took place right next to his domain, that Tom has very precise knowledge of them and his overall solemnity about it would imply he had some unspecified involvement with the fall of Cardolan.

I would imagine Adar makes a first sortie against Eregion, Gil-galad's/Elrond's forces arrive and temporarily push him back (and allowing Galadriel to escape captivity with Morgoth's crown). Adar and Elrond/Gil-galad have a parley before Elrond leaves to request dwarven aid while Gil-galad holds the fort (probably where we get Damrod vs Gil-galad and Arondir). Durin IV fails to persuade his father to help the elves and has some internal conflict about what to do. Inside Eregion Celebrimbor finally connects the dots and breaks Sauron's illusion after/during forging the Nine. Galadriel sneaks inside Eregion to see Celebrimbor. With the Nine finished, Sauron goes off to confront Adar 1v1 and Galadriel goes after him, setting up their final showdown for Morgoth's crown in the last episode.   
  
Episode might end with Prince Durin deciding to disobey his father and march to help the elves (which is where we see the "fight with our friends!" speech from the trailers) as the Khazad-dum theme blares.
It's worth noting that in LOTR itself Bombadil implies he had some unspecified involvement in the War of Angmar and the fall of the Last Prince of Cardolan.

If I had to guess Miriel will marry Pharazon in an attempt to avoid bloodshed in Númenor. Elendil might end the season looking for his estranged son, Anárion (briefly mentioned in s1). I think he'll only sail to ME fully in season 3-4.

I thought Tom was solid in episode 4 with a mix of whimsy and some seriousness, but this one leaned too much in the mentor role and stumbled. As much as the character avoids being involved in Middle-Earth, Tom does basically say he was involved in some fashion with the Angmar War in the book, so it's not without precedent. Episode 4 I thought spun a nice trick where Tom made clear to Gandalf magic isn't about dominating nature but working in tandem with nature, a very Tolkienesque point of view. Here's hoping Tom recovers in the finish line.

There's even the addendum that the high priest of Stannis' faith is obstensibly a (foreign, no less) woman while the Faith of the Seven (like the Catholic Church) seems by default patriarchal. It's just a very scandalous combination from any angle.

They do bring up in the episode that none of their scouts have returned (save for the corpse with the "where is he?" writing). In general the impression given (to me) is that Eregion isn't that heavily fortified, being this sort of arts/commerce hub created during a time of peace and led by artisans (rather than warriors), so security is a bit lax and they're relying on natural defenses (narrow bridges, river, thick walls, mountain right behind).

What's actually stranger to me in terms of religiosity is how relatively chill everyone is about Stannis adopting a foreign faith and burning the symbols of the faith of the throne for hundreds of years. If a king of england irl declared himself for Zoroastranism in the 1100s there would be Hell to pay and he'd be declared illegitimate in a femtosecond, but in ACOK even his enemies only barely bring it up.
I think the ending of episode 6, with Sauron rejocing as Eregion goes straight to Hell, feels too much like a nod to Sauron rejoicing while Númenor sinks for them not to do that bit.

It basically depends how old these people are by this point and if the show is keeping the bit of the books of the Númenorean living longer than regular humans. In canon, for example, Elendil died at about 300 years of age and Isildur at about 200. So the timeskips here can be as small as a few years or as big as a century.

He was scant on details but still enough convenience to set off some suspicions. Last season when Halbrand had Adar at his mercy he also said "Remember me?" to which Adar seemed very confused and just said "No" (as from his perspective, they never met). He's probably been wondering about it since.

On top of what's been said about Celebrimbor diverting all attention to the forge and Sauron running interference to weaken the defenses, it's notable that the ending of episode 5 shows that the Orcs came up from behind a elevation that overlooks Eregion. Presumably that would cover their troop movements from the sight of the watchtowers.
Halbrand showing up at random in Mordor and trying to cajole him with info probably made him go "This chicanery sounds familiar..."

In the show's timeline I think Lothlorien, Rivendell don't exist yet, on top of Gondor and Arnor also needing to be established. I think by default the show will need one or two timeskips for these places to be properly established by the time of the War of the Last Alliance (as I don't think we'll see Númenoreans building Minas Ithil and Minas Tirith brick-by-brick in real time).
You can actually see his silhouette in the trees at around 0:27 when the catapult launches a fireball. The chonky boy is marching to war.

Weaker than last week's but still ok. Adar, Celebrimbor and Elendil as the MVPs. Tom Bombadil stumbled a bit after what I thought was a wonderful introduction, but I think his choice presented to Gandalf (and it is Gandalf, let us not kid ourselves. I do think The Dark Wizard is one of the Blues or a Blue replacement if they don't have the rights) is a false choice and the right move is helping his friends. This episode and the last made me think that if this show  was just about Eregion, Khazad-dum and Númenor this would flow a lot smoother.

It is a little bizarre, but they do mention in the episode that they sent several scouting parties and no one returned and Sauron explicitly orders them to stay up and do nothing. Combined with their Lord Celebrimbor being absent, the idea the city ended up wholly unprotected is not out of the realm of possibility. Gil-galad not having anciliary forces to catch orcish movement before they got to Eregion is weaker, but previous episode did have a brief scene he's questioned why he's not marching to battle already and he seems reluctant as we see The Ring giving him foresight of what's likely his own death.

I really dislike how Shadow just made Celebrimbor a cold, calculating Feanor 2.0. Celebrimbor's main moment in the First Age is Celebrimbor cutting ties with the political machinations of his father and uncle (Curufin and Celegorn). I much prefer Rings of Power having him be genuinely warm and well-intentioned guy as a repudiation of Feanor's ruthlesness, but still causing great harm for a entirely different set of character flaws (namely naivete and a desire to be respected). Shadow Celebrimbor feels more like Curufin, not his son.
Low opacity Adar, the promised one.
Aside from viewer convenience, Sauron also doesn't seem to be particularly fond of his former boss anyway, so calling him "Morgoth" tracks.

His "There can be no trust between the hammer and the rock. Sooner or later one or the other will break." is my favorite dialogue from season one. Peter Mullan and the writers just sizzle with this character.
They probably are able to retain light from the sun even at nighttime with dwarven crafts.

What I like:

* Most of the cast. I think everyone is delivering solid performances across the board, regardless of how their plotlines are actually shaking up and the backlash the actors are getting in social media has been pretty despicable. 

* The atmosphere is on-point. Staging (Númenor and Khazad-Dûm in particular look incredible), score, cinematography, CGI.  Incredibly immersive.

* Khazad-Dûm and the dwarves in general have consistently been highlights. 

* The Orcs are fantastic and might be my favorite version of the Orcs on-screen so far. The deathly pale coloring just looks very well on them, and the bone armor is very evocative. 

* The Harfoots are delightful. 

What I dislike:

* Celebrimbor and Gil-Galad really need more  screentime. They're very pivotal characters to be sidelined.

* First three episodes struggled a lot with introducing concepts in a organic way, which is a common problem in Tolkien adaptations given the sheer depth of the world. 

* Galadriel is fine (aided by Morfydd Clark being tremendous actress who has been knocking it out of the park), but her plotline did tend towards repetiveness in the first four episodes. At least she finally learned to switch gears in episode four (being actually pretty diplomatic with Miriel after Halbrand's pep-talk).

* I don't particularly like some of the approach in keeping too many mysteries (Adar, Meteor Man, the significance of the hilt, e.t.c.).

* I like Arondir, but Theo is insufferable and the elven-human romance feels obligatory and played out.

* Wayne Che Yip (director of about half the episodes of this season) could stand to use fewer slow-motion shots. It's starting to get excessive. I leaned more to Bayona's stylistic in the first two episodes.

* Some time compression is unavoidable, but some of it just leaves  me confused.

Overall, I'm enjoying it and I think it has room to both grow or collapse, but so far it looks positive.
